items: A String is a Python data type
A String is a sequence of individual characters, like "c" or "?"
Characters are arranged in a particular order in a string
For instance, "tale" and "teal" are different strings, although they contain the same four characters

lecture_blocks.title: Accessing the Individual Characters in a String

items: Some programming tasks require you to access the individual characters that are contained within a string.
You can isolate individual characters within a string by using a "for" loop. The target variable in your loop will assume each character in your string one at a time.
The following loop prints out each of the characters in "tale" on its own line.

code_cells.content:
for c in "tale":
  print(c)

segments.text: Use a loop like the one above to count how many times the letter "s" appears in the string "sally sells sea shells by the sea shore."

items: Another way to access a string is to use an index value.
Index values refer to individual characters
You use square brackets to index into strings, with the numerical index value inside the brackets
Index values start at zero for the first character, one for the second, etc.
You can use negative values to count back from the end

code_cells.content:
s="Superman"
print(s[0]) # first character "S"
print(s[2]) # third character "p"
print(s[4]) # fifth character "r"
print(s[-2]) # second to last character "a"
print(s[-1]) # last character "n"
print(s[-8]) # first character "S"
# print(s[8]) # this will be out of range

segments.text: The "len" function will tell us the length of a string.
If you index into a string with an index more than one minus the length, it will generate an error.

code_cells.content:
s="Superman"
print(len(s))

lecture_blocks.title: Iterating Over a String Using Indexing

segments.text: As we have seen, you can iterate over a string using the "in" statement and a "for" loop
You can also loop using the index, but you will need to specify a range using the "len" function.

code_cells.content:
# looping using "in"
word="teal"
for c in word:
  print(c)

# looping using "range" and "len" and indexing
# works out the same.
word="teal"
# note if given one parameter, range gives values between
# zero and one minus that parameter
for i in range(len(word)):
  print(i, word[i])

segments.text: Use string indexing and the len and range functions to count the combined number of "S" and "s" characters in the string "Superman sings soulfully in the shower." Use a "for" loop.
Use string indexing to print out the string "Superman sings soulfully in the shower" in reverse. Print the reversed version on a single line.

items: Strings are an immutable data type. This means that they cannot be changed once they are created.
This may seem counter-intuitive, since we can (and have) been doing things like the following:

segments.text: However, what happens in the code above is that Python creates a string "Cheddar" and sets the variable "cheese" to point to it. Then it creates another string "Brie" and changes the variable so it now points to "Brie". The original string "Cheddar" is still in memory but no variable points to it any more.
Since strings are immutable, you can't change the characters in them. The following won't work:

code_cells.content:
cheese="Cheddar"
print(f"The cheese is {cheese}")
cheese="Brie"
print(f"The cheese is {cheese}")

name="Mary"
# try to change it to "Gary"
name[0]="G"

segments.text: Because strings are immutable, you can't change them by changing the characters in them. You need to construct a new string.
Suppose you want to change every vowel in a word to an underscore. Suppose the word is "hello". You could try to do the following, but it won't work.
Instead, you have to do something like the following:

code_cells.content:
word="hello"
word[1]="_"
word[4]="_"

word="hello"
new_word=""
for c in word:
    if c.lower() in "aeiou": # if is a vowel
      new_word+="_" # put an underscore at the end
    else:
      new_word+=c # put the non-vowel at the end
# we can then set the old variable to the same
# value as the new one
# it now points to the new string
word=new_word
print(word)

lecture_blocks.title: The ord Function: Getting the ASCII Value of a Character

items: If you recall, Python uses the ASCII coding scheme to store characters.
The ord() function gives you the ascii value of a character given as its argument
for instance, ord("A") returns 65

code_cells.content: print(ord("A"))

lecture_blocks.title: The chr() function: Gets a Character from an ASCII Code

items: The chr() function is the reverse of the ORD function
Given an ASCII code, it returns a character
For instance, chr(65) returns "A"

code_cells.content:
print(chr(65))
print(chr(ord("A")))

items: We already know a few string functions: len, chr, and ord
There are many more useful string functions
The min and max functions get the smallest and largest characters in a string, based on their ASCII codes.

code_cells.content:
print(max("python"))
print(min("python"))
print(max("123"))
print(min("123"))

items: You can extract substrings of a string by giving the first index and the last index (plus one) desired separated by a colon

code_cells.content:
full_name="Mirabel Madrigal"
first_name=full_name[:7]
last_name=full_name[8:]
print(first_name)
print(last_name)
s=full_name[8:11:2]
print(s)

l=full_name.split()
print(l)
l="James Earl Jones".split()
print(l)

items: You use brackets to slice a string
The syntax is as follows:
You must supply at least a starting or ending value
Substrings start at the start value specified and end at one minus the end value
Omitting a start value means you start at the beginning
Omitting a end value means you go all the way to the end
The syntax is similar to the range() function

code_cells.content: substring=bigstring[start:end:step]
substring=bigstring[start:end:step]

# Slicing Examples
s="Superman sings in the shower."
print(s[0:8]) # Superman
print(s[:8]) # Superman
print(s[9:14]) # sings
print(s[:5]) # Super
print(s[9:]) # sings in the shower.
print(s[-7:]) # shower.
print(s[0:len(s):3]) # Seasgit or

items: We already know about two string operators, "+" and "*"
The "+" operator concanenates two strings, that is, puts the second at the end of the first
The "*" operator repeats a string a number of times (specified as an integer)

code_cells.content:
a="Hello"
b=", "
c="World"
d="!"
e=a+b+c+d
print(e)
print("Repeat Me "*5)

lecture_blocks.title: Testing for Substrings Using "in" and "not in"

items: a in b tests if string a is found inside string b
a not in b tests for the opposite

code_cells.content:
names="Pedro Alma Julieta Papa Bruno Augustin Felix Isabela Luisa Mirabel"
print("Luisa" in names) # True
print("Louisa" in names) # False
print("Alma" not in names) # False
print("Ann" not in names) # True

items: A method is a function that belongs to a Python object.
We will be covering objects more later
Strings are objects and have methods
The syntax to call methods uses dot notation similar to that we have seen with modules, as follows:

code_cells.content: stringvariable.method(arguments)
stringvariable.method(arguments)

items: String testing methods allow you to test patterns in a string
For instance, the "isdigit" method, if given a character, returns True if it is a numeric digit and False otherwise
If "isdigit" is given a string, it returns true if all of the characters in that string are digits

code_cells.content:
print("5".isdigit())
print("a".isdigit())
print("1234".isdigit())
print("a123".isdigit())

x="3"
y="a3"
print(x.isdigit())
print(y.isdigit())

items: isalnum(): True if all characters are alphanumeric
isalpha(): True if all characters are alphabetic
isdigit(): True if all characters are digits
islower(): True if all alphabetic characters are lower case
isupper(): True if all alphabetic characters are upper case
isspace(): True if all characters are "whitespace"

code_cells.content:
print(ord("\n"))
print("\n".isspace())
print(" ".isspace())
print("\t".isspace())
print("\n\n\n")
s="Hello\nThere\nWorld!"
print(s)

segments.text: Write a program that counts the numbers of spaces, digits, vowels and consonants in a string that the user inputs. Print the counts of each.

items: lower(): returns a lowercase version of a string
upper(): returns an uppercase version of a string
rstrip(): removes whitespace at the end of a string
lstrip(): removes whitespace at the beginning of a string
strip(): removes whitespace at both the beginning and end of a string
capitalize(): capitalizes a string (first character upper case)
title(): capitalizes the first character of each word in a string
swapcase(): turns lower case to upper and vice versa in a string

code_cells.content:
print("HELLO".lower()) # hello
print("hello".upper()) # HELLO
print("hello   ".rstrip())
print("  hello".lstrip())
print("  hello  ".strip())
print("hello".capitalize()) # Hello
print("hello there".title()) # "Hello There"
print("Hello There".title().swapcase()) #  "hELLO tHERE"

x="HELLO"
x=x.lower()
print(x)

items: You can find the location of a string inside another string using the find() method
It will return the index of the first occurence of the substring within a string.
If it isn't found, it will return -1

code_cells.content:
sentence="Like finding a needle in a haystack!"
location=sentence.find("needle")
print(location)
l2=sentence.find("sword")
print(l2)

items: The replace() method will replace all occurences of a substring in a string with a new string
An example is the following:

code_cells.content:
text="""Voldemort had one goal in life:
to kill Harry Potter.
Voldemort hated Harry."""
print(text)
newtext=text.replace("Voldemort","He who should not be named")
print(newtext)
